Limits: the positive view is offered as a hunch, the psychopath is a stipulated case, and the lecture does not restate the Reason View of Freedom Within Reason ([LIT-685](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-685.md)). |

| [LIT-1402](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1402.md) v2 | The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin | Franklin (written 1771–1790; first published 1791). The memoir of his life to 1757. Part Three holds the anecdote the Benjamin Franklin effect is named for: to win over a hostile new member of the Pennsylvania Assembly, Franklin asked to borrow a scarce book from his library, returned it with thanks, and the man thereafter spoke to him with civility and "manifested a readiness to serve me on all occasions". Franklin gives it as "another instance of the truth of an old maxim", "He that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another, than he whom you yourself have obliged", and as a lesson in prudence. Around it the memoir is a record of how he got others to act with him: undogmatic speech, projects presented as his friends', and opinion prepared in print and through the Junto's satellite clubs. | Active — read 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1360](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1360.md)) in full, from Project Gutenberg eBook [#148](https://github.com/dmarx/nucleation/issues/148) (Harvard Classics, 1909); worth reading as the source of the Benjamin Franklin effect and, around it, a first-hand manual of influence: modest speech, projects put forward as "a scheme of a number of friends", opinion prepared in print and spread through the Junto's clubs "as arising in each of them". Read it knowing that it is a memoir written decades after the events, for posterity and in part from memory without papers; that the borrowed-book story is one instance of an "old maxim", given as prudence, with the member unnamed and the effect reported by the man who sought it; and that the edition's chronology list has errors the memoir itself contradicts. |
| [LIT-1408](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1408.md) v4 | Intergroup Contact Theory | Pettigrew (1998). Reviews Allport's contact hypothesis (equal status, common goals, cooperation, authority support) and names four problems: selection bias in cross-sectional studies, an expanding list of conditions that are facilitating rather than essential, no account of process, and no account of how effects generalize. Proposes four processes (learning about the outgroup, changed behaviour as the precursor of attitude change, affective ties, and ingroup reappraisal, whose outcome it calls "deprovincialization"), three sequential strategies for generalization (decategorization, salient categorization, recategorization), and a longitudinal contact theory in which Allport's four conditions and a fifth, friendship potential, are essential and other factors facilitating. In the author's European surveys the path from outgroup friendship to less prejudice is stronger than the reverse. | Active — read 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1408](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1408.md)) in full, from an Annual Reviews PDF of the chapter on Serendip Studio, Bryn Mawr College's science-education site (https://serendipstudio.org/oneworld/system/files/annurev.psych_.49.1.65-2.pdf); worth reading as the review that turned Allport's contact hypothesis into a theory with four processes (learning, changed behavior, affective ties, ingroup reappraisal), a staged account of generalization and a fifth condition, friendship potential. Read it knowing that its processes are proposed rather than tested, that its causal evidence is mostly the author's cross-sectional European surveys, that "deprovincialization" occurs once and rests on one unpublished analysis of national pride, and that its model still treats Allport's four conditions as essential, which the 2006 meta-analysis ([LIT-1413](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1413.md)) does not bear out. |
| [LIT-1413](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1413.md) v3 | A Meta-Analytic Test of Intergroup Contact Theory | Pettigrew & Tropp (2006). A meta-analysis of 515 studies (713 independent samples, 250,089 participants, 38 countries, through 2000) finds that intergroup contact typically reduces intergroup prejudice (random-effects r ≈ −.21; 94% of samples negative). Samples without choice of contact show larger effects, and the more rigorous studies larger ones (experiments −.34), though for racial and ethnic targets experiments show no advantage. Five of six publication-bias checks find none; Vevea and Hedges's model, adjusted, leaves no significant overall effect but a significant one for well-controlled designs. Effects generalize to the whole outgroup and, in few tests, beyond. Allport's optimal conditions enhance the effect (structured programs −.29 against −.20) but work as a bundle and are not essential to it. | Active — read 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1407](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1407.md)) in full, from the published article's PDF on a University of Pennsylvania Wharton site (https://ideas.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/Pettigrew-Tropp.pdf); worth reading as the meta-analysis of 515 studies (713 samples) that established a reliable negative association between face-to-face intergroup contact and prejudice (r ≈ −.21, −.34 in experiments) and showed Allport's conditions to enhance it without being needed. Read it knowing that most of its samples are cross-sectional surveys of reported contact, that one of its six publication-bias checks (Vevea and Hedges) leaves no significant overall effect, and that the larger effects of rigorous designs come from non-racial targets: for racial and ethnic samples experiments give −.22, the overall mean. |
| [LIT-1419](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1419.md) v2 | Liking a Person as a Function of Doing Him a Favour | Jecker & Landy (1969). The first experimental test of the Benjamin Franklin effect. Participants won money in a concept-formation task; afterwards one group was asked by the experimenter to return it as a personal favour (he was paying out of his own pocket), one was asked by a departmental secretary on behalf of the psychology department, and one was not asked. Those who did the experimenter a personal favour rated him most likable. Standardly read as a dissonance effect: one justifies a favour by liking its recipient. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-23, not read. A lawful full text was sought on 2026-10-29 and not reached. OpenAlex reports it closed with no repository copy; the SAGE page is paywalled; a web search found only secondary accounts and abstract listings (Scilit). It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied, and its summary remains secondary. No NOTE is filed. |

| [LIT-1428](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1428.md) | Psychopathy as a Clinical and Empirical Construct | Hare & Neumann (2008), Annual Review of Clinical Psychology 4:217–246. The PCL-R's items form four correlated factors, Interpersonal, Affective, Lifestyle and Antisocial, explained by one superordinate factor; psychopathy is dimensional, and no component, affective or antisocial, is more essential than the others. Cleckley's Clinical Profile, drawn from an unrepresentative sample, should not be the test of the construct. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1094](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1094.md)): in full, from the copy Hare posts on his own site. Worth reading as the authors' own statement of what the construct is, made while defending it against the charge that the PCL-R has "drifted" from Cleckley. The PCL-R's 20 items fall, 18 of them, into four correlated factors: Interpersonal and Affective (together Factor 1) and Lifestyle and Antisocial (together Factor 2). A single superordinate factor explains them, and the authors hold that no component, the affective one included, is more essential than the others. That is the sharpest constraint the record has on borrowing only the affective features of psychopathy for a corporation. Hare receives royalties from the PCL-R. |

| [LIT-1713](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1713.md) | Responsibility to Future Generations: A Moral Reframing Strategy for Combatting Climate Change | Syropoulos, Kraft-Todd, Mah, Markowitz & Young (2023). Thirteen studies (six main, seven supplementary; N = 161,633) on felt responsibility to future generations (RFG). In Eurobarometer data from 34 European countries (N = 109,513), a majority in 33 agreed "We need to reform to benefit future generations even if that means making some sacrifices now"; agreement barely related to ideology, age or gender (meta-r .03 to .07) and weakly to subjective status (.13). In US samples RFG was endorsed more than responsibility to reduce one's own contribution to climate change (RCC), correlated with conservatism half as strongly (meta-r −.21 against −.45), and predicted self-reported proenvironmental behaviour, concern and policy support. In a preregistered experiment (N = 3,175), five brief interventions (a letter to a person born today, legacy reflection, reflection on past generations' sacrifices, a park video, a 385-word excerpt of *What We Owe the Future*) each raised RFG and proenvironmental intentions by small amounts (d = .14 to .54); only the letter raised donations. Reflection on past sacrifices raised RFG but not RCC. All outcomes are self-reports or a small donation. status_note: worth reading as the largest study of felt responsibility to future generations, its spread and its political neutrality, and as the record's only experiment comparing legacy, reciprocity, a particular future person and an impersonal longtermist text as routes to it; read in place of Syropoulos and Markowitz 2021. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1293](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1293.md)), in place of [LIT-1741](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1741.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the largest study of felt responsibility to future generations, its spread and its political neutrality, and as the record's only experiment comparing legacy, reciprocity, a particular future person and an impersonal longtermist text as routes to it; read in place of Syropoulos and Markowitz 2021. |
| [LIT-1717](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1717.md) | Leaving a Legacy: Intergenerational Allocations of Benefits and Burdens | Six experiments (N = 76, 101, 64, 32, 131, 92; U.S. undergraduates, MBA students and university staff) on how the valence of what is passed on affects concern for one's legacy and generosity to future others. Framing climate change as leaving burdens, rather than using up benefits, raised a generativity scale built from items about being remembered and living on (4.90 vs 4.10), direct concern with one's legacy, felt responsibility and affinity toward future generations, and ethical concern; recalling one's own past burden allocation raised moral emotions. In allocation tasks people favoured themselves more with benefits than with burdens. The difference appeared only when the recipient was in the future (not in a dictator-game version with a present recipient), and only when the allocator was a party to the trade-off (not when allocating between two other people). One item on ethical considerations statistically accounted for the first of these. The authors read the pattern as legacy concern, which they define as the wish to extend the self beyond death, engaged more by leaving burdens than by withholding benefits. Legacy concern was measured only in the attitude studies, never in the allocation studies. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1273](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1273.md)), in place of [LIT-1716](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1716.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the legacy programme's fullest experimental statement before the 2012 mortality studies, and as the record's only second-hand source for Wade-Benzoni 2006 ([LIT-1716](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1716.md)). Read it knowing that legacy concern and generosity are never measured in the same study, and that the generosity effects sit in one cell: people keep more benefits for themselves when the other person will receive them later. |
| [LIT-1729](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1729.md) | Empirical Approaches to Altruism | The SEP survey of the empirical egoism–altruism debate, revised in 2025. On the standard account, altruism needs an ultimate desire for another's well-being; biological and social-science senses of "altruism" settle nothing about it. Batson's experiments make a strong case against the aversive-arousal and social-punishment versions of egoism. Self-other merging is a different challenge: only numerical identity with the helped person would make helping egoistic, and none of the four measures used by Cialdini et al. and Batson et al. (IOS, "we", perceived similarity, trait-rating difference) tests for it. The authors report that Batson et al. (1997) avoided Cialdini's methodological problems and found empathy's role "clearly evident", and that a preregistered study (N = 680) supports the empathy–helping link. Altruism is still not shown: divine punishment, principlism, non-moral norms, and habitual or Pavlovian helping remain to be ruled out. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1274](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1274.md)), in place of [LIT-1700](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1700.md) and [LIT-1728](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1728.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the shortest neutral account of the 1997 merging exchange the record holds: it quotes both papers' measures, and it argues that a merging criterion must be one of numerical identity to matter for egoism. | [LIT-1743](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1743.md) | Preregistered Replication and Extension of “Moral Hypocrisy: Social Groups and the Flexibility of Virtue” | Robertson, Akles & Van Bavel (2024). Two preregistered experiments (minimal groups n = 590; partisans n = 577) did not replicate intergroup moral hypocrisy; the minimal-group contrast is statistically equivalent to zero. In minimal groups, in-group favouritism in fairness judgments rose with collective identification and was not significant overall (p = .07); partisans judged out-party members' identical selfish acts less fair (p = .003). | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1245](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1245.md)) from the authors' accepted manuscript on OSF; worth reading as the record's only preregistered evidence on minimal-group favouritism. | [LIT-1748](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1748.md) | The Psychology of Existential Risk: Moral Judgments about Human Extinction | Schubert, Caviola & Faber (2019). Five studies (N = 2,507 as stated) of Parfit's three outcomes: no catastrophe, 80% of humanity killed, 100% killed. Most laypeople judge extinction bad and say it must be prevented, but only 19–37% of those ranking the outcomes in the expected order judge the step from 80% to 100% worse than the step from none to 80%. More do when the victims are zebras, when the catastrophe sterilizes rather than kills, or when told to consider the long-term future (39–50%). A majority (67–77%) do only when told the surviving future would be long and utopian. People recruited as existential-risk mitigators do so unprompted (86%). The authors conclude that laypeople attend to immediate harm to fellow humans and neglect the long-term consequences. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1270](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1270.md)) from the publisher's PDF (CC BY), without the supplementary materials; worth reading as the first experiment on how far lay moral concern reaches past the living, and what makes it reach further: salience of the future, its quality, and less sympathy with the victims. |
| [LIT-1749](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1749.md) | Population ethical intuitions | Caviola, Althaus, Mogensen & Goodwin (preprint 2021; Cognition 2022). Nine experiments (N = 5,776 as stated) on lay population axiology. For a fixed population to be better existing than not, people require more happiness than suffering: about 75% happy people, still about 61% when the two are stated to be exactly equally intense. Yet adding one extremely happy person to a world is judged as good as adding one extremely unhappy person is bad, so people reject neutrality and the procreation asymmetry. They prefer larger happy and smaller unhappy populations when averages are fixed, but the preference for more happy people fades and reverses at a billion. With totals fixed they prefer higher averages, and in conflicts averagism tends to win, even favouring adding near-maximally unhappy people who raise the average. Prompts to reflect move judgements toward totalism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1267](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1267.md)) from the authors' PsyArXiv preprint (osf.io/wdbr8, OSF file of 2021-04-01); worth reading as the main experimental evidence on whether ordinary judgement is person-affecting or impersonal about merely possible people, and on how weak its totalism is at large numbers. |
| [LIT-1766](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1766.md) | Recategorization and Prosocial Behavior: Common In-Group Identity and a Dual Identity | A review of the common in-group identity model applied to helping. Recategorizing two groups as one removes in-group bias in helping: in a laboratory study, help to an original out-group member rose to the in-group level; at a football stadium, White fans complied with a Black interviewer's request more often when he wore their university's hat (59% vs 36%). Commons-dilemma studies show the same for cooperation. But the form of the shared identity matters. White students helped a Black student least when he called himself a Black person or a Black Colgate student (a dual identity), and most when he called himself a Colgate student. In the second study, empathic concern partly mediated that effect on helping; attitudes did not. The authors trace the dual identity's cost to majority members projecting their group's standards onto the superordinate category, and to identity threat. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1286](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1286.md)), in place of [LIT-1710](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1710.md) and [LIT-1709](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1709.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the model's authors' own account of how an enlarged "we" extends helping across group lines, with the qualification that the "we" which helps is the helper's version of it. |
| [LIT-1786](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1786.md) | Group-level self-definition and self-investment: A hierarchical (multicomponent) model of in-group identification | In-group identification has five components on two correlated dimensions. Group-level self-definition is individual self-stereotyping (seeing oneself as like the average member) and in-group homogeneity; group-level self-investment is solidarity, satisfaction and centrality. In confirmatory factor analyses of Dutch, European and university identification in two cohorts (N = 464, 363), this model fit better than one-factor, two-factor and cognitive-versus-affective alternatives; the two dimensions correlated .61 to .77. Prospectively, the components predicted different things: centrality predicted perceived threat, homogeneity perceived intergroup difference, and, facing evidence of their group's misdeeds, self-stereotyping predicted group-based guilt while satisfaction and centrality predicted legitimizing the misdeeds. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1262](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1262.md)), in place of [LIT-1795](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1795.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the direct test of whether identification splits into a self-definition and a caring dimension: it does, and they can work against each other. |

Princeton first-year students took part in either a peer-oriented discussion that exposed pluralistic ignorance about drinking or an individual-oriented discussion of responsible decisions. Four to six months later the peer-oriented group reported fewer drinks a week (3.10 against 5.05; p = .05). Their estimates of the average student's comfort with drinking did not differ by condition. What differed was that, in the control condition, students high in fear of negative evaluation drank above average whatever they thought of peers. The authors infer that exposure weakened the norm's prescriptive force without changing what it prescribed. Men closed the gap between their own and the average student's comfort, but by revising their estimate of others, not their own attitude, the reverse of Prentice and Miller's 1993 finding. | Active — read in full 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1439](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1439.md)) from the published article as downloaded from Wiley and posted on Stanford SPARQ's site (https://sparq.stanford.edu/sites/g/files/sbiybj19021/files/media/file/schroeder_prentice_1998_-_exposing_pluralistic_ignorance.pdf); worth reading as the field test of exposing pluralistic ignorance, and as the nearest read source for Prentice and Miller 1993 ([LIT-1370](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1370.md)), which it restates and in part fails to replicate. | [LIT-2658](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2658.md) | Attributability, Answerability, and Accountability: In Defense of a Unified Account | Smith (2012). Attributability, Answerability, and Accountability: In Defense of a Unified Account. Ethics 122(3): 575-589. A reply to Shoemaker's (2011) three conceptions of responsibility. Smith argues that answerability, being open to a demand to justify one's attitudes and conduct, is the only kind of moral responsibility. What Shoemaker calls attributability is not responsibility at all, since we withhold aretaic labels from agents who are not answerable (the OCD case). What he calls accountability is answerability where a specific obligation to others has been violated. The different responses warranted differ by the seriousness of the failure, the relationship and the blamer's standing, which belong to the ethics of blame, not to the conditions of responsibility. Filed as a neighbour for Watson's "Two Faces of Responsibility", whose distinction it disputes. | Active — read in full 2026-11-16 ([NOTE-2008](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2008.md)) from a copy of the published article on an MIT moral-psychology reading-group page (https://www.mit.edu/~shaslang/mprg/ASmithAAA.pdf). | [LIT-2662](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2662.md) v2 | Moral Luck | Nagel (1979). Moral Luck. Mortal Questions, ch. 3. A revised version of his 1976 reply to Williams. Ordinary excuses rest on a condition that we are assessable only for what we control. Applied consistently, it erodes nearly all moral judgment, because what we are judged for depends on four kinds of luck: resultant (how things turn out), constitutive (the kind of person one is), circumstantial (the situations one faces) and causal (how one is determined by antecedent circumstances). Nagel holds that this is a genuine paradox, like scepticism, and not an error repaired by a refined condition. He rejects both paring action down to the will and the compatibilist reply, and traces the problem to the clash between the internal view of agency and the external view of acts as events. "In a sense", it has no solution. | Active — Read in full 2026-11-16 ([NOTE-2015](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2015.md)) from an anthology reprint of the Mortal Questions text, posted as a course file on the University of Athens e-class site (course PHILOSOPHY921). Worth reading: the canonical statement of the problem of moral luck and its four kinds, and the source of the record's terms for them. |

| [LIT-2673](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2673.md) v2 | Coercion | Anderson (2006, rev. 2023). Coercion. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. A survey of coercion as a technique of coercers and a reason for coercees. Its §3.2 finds no general theory of how coercion affects the coerced party's responsibility. The effect varies with the act and its moral context and runs mostly through justification, with excuse reserved mainly for a will that breaks down. Moral tests (Wertheimer, Pallikkathayil, lesser evil) and psychological ones (Feinberg) each cover only part of the field. Because coercion is strategic, the responsibility rule shapes coercers' incentives. It reports Galoob and Sheley's defence for a target whose decisional authority a coercive controller has usurped, and White's view that a conditional threat makes the coercee responsible for preventing what the coercer threatens. Bears on [CLAIM-708](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-708.md), [CLAIM-709](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-709.md) and [CASE-279](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-279.md). Emotional manipulation is excluded by stipulation. | Active — Skimmed 2026-11-16 ([NOTE-2014](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2014.md)) from the plato.stanford.edu HTML (substantive revision of 23 Jan 2023): §§2.1.3, 2.5, 3.1, 3.2 and most of 3.3 read in full; the history (§1), the threats-and-baselines analysis (§§2.1–2.4) and §3.4 skipped. Worth reading as the record's source on how coercion bears on the coerced party's responsibility (§3.2), including a reported defence for targets of coercive control. |

| [LIT-2695](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2695.md) | Moral Luck | Nelkin (2004, rev. 2025). Moral Luck. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. The problem of moral luck, set out from Williams (1976) and Nagel (1979) as a conflict between the Control Principle, that we are assessable only for what depends on our control, and everyday judgments that assess people for what depends on luck. It restates Nagel's four kinds (resultant, circumstantial, constitutive, causal) and surveys the responses: explaining the appearance away (the epistemic argument; Williams's agent-regret and Wolf's virtue of taking responsibility as appropriate feeling, not differential blame), Williams's Postscript (keep the Control Principle for "morality" and care about ethics instead), and accepting moral luck with or without revising practice. Read as the stand-in for Williams's paper. | Active — skimmed 2026-11-16 ([NOTE-2023](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2023.md)) from the plato.stanford.edu HTML, substantive revision of 20 Jan 2025; filed and read as the stand-in for Williams, "Moral Luck" ([LIT-2714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2714.md), Unfetched). Conflict and Control: Gender Symmetry and Asymmetry in Domestic Violence. Violence Against Women 12(11): 1003-1018. DOI 10.1177/1077801206293328. Defines four types of partner violence by the control context of the couple, not by the violence (intimate terrorism, violent resistance, situational couple violence, mutual violent control), and shows in Frieze's 1970s court, shelter and survey sample that intimate terrorism is almost all men's and found in agency samples, while situational couple violence is near gender-symmetric and dominates general surveys. Read as the stand-in for Johnson's 2008 book ([LIT-2715](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2715.md)) on the typology the exchange "Assess Depp Heard Abuse" cites (A3 §2, §5). | Active |

| [LIT-2712](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2712.md) | Coercive Control: Update and Review | Stark and Hester (2019). Coercive Control: Update and Review. Violence Against Women 25(1): 81-104. DOI 10.1177/1077801218816191. Reviews the new coercive-control offences in England/Wales and Scotland and research since 2009, holding that "Coercive control is not a type of violence": Stark's coercion (force or threats) and control (deprivation, exploitation, command) produce a condition of unfreedom experienced as entrapment, in perhaps a third of cases without notable violence, and the level of control predicts harms including post-separation violence. Read as the stand-in for Stark's 2007 book ([LIT-2675](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2675.md)), which the exchange "Assess Depp Heard Abuse" cites (A3 §3). | Active |
| [LIT-2714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2714.md) v2 | Moral Luck | Williams (1976). Moral Luck. Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society, Supplementary Volume 50: 115–135. Not read; known through the SEP "Moral Luck" entry and Nagel's reply. The paper that named moral luck. Its Gauguin case is a decision whose justification, if any, depends on an outcome beyond the agent's control. It introduces agent-regret: the faultless lorry driver's first-person regret, expressed partly in a willingness to compensate, which "cannot merely be eliminated by the consideration that it was not his fault". Williams's 1993 Postscript reads it as keeping morality immune to luck at the cost of its supreme importance, in favour of "ethics". The exchange cites it for moral residue and agent-regret (A7 §2) and for moral luck (A7 §7). | Unfetched — the publisher's copy, at https://academic.oup.com/aristoteliansupp/article-lookup/doi/10.1093/aristoteliansupp/50.1.115 (reached from doi.org on 2026-11-16), was stopped by a Cloudflare challenge ("Just a moment...", HTTP 403) and not retried. Whether it is open access is unconfirmed: one index result called it open access. No course or author copy was found by search (course handouts discuss it but do not reproduce it). Read in its place: the SEP "Moral Luck" entry (Nelkin, filed as a neighbour), which quotes the lorry-driver passage and reports agent-regret and the 1993 Postscript, and Nagel's reply ([LIT-2662](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2662.md), read), whose notes 3 and 4 report Williams's Gauguin case and his term "agent-regret". |

| [LIT-2717](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2717.md) v2 | An Updated and Revised Dyadic Model of Partner Violence | Mazinani and O'Connor (2026). An Updated and Revised Dyadic Model of Partner Violence. Behavioral Sciences (Basel) 16(9): 1468. DOI 10.3390/bs16091468. A selective review that maps risk markers for physical IPV from eight meta-analyses onto Bartholomew and Cobb's dyadic model. The most consistent and largest associations are in the relationship context (prior aggression, emotional abuse, dissatisfaction); communication skills and empathy are inversely associated. The authors hold that relational framing implies neither symmetric control nor shared responsibility, and that Johnson's typology is complementary. Registered from the exchange "Assess Depp Heard Abuse" (A5 §6), which summarizes it accurately. Read 2026-11-16. | Active — Read 2026-11-16 from the open-access full text in Europe PMC (PMC13603925). | [LIT-2720](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2720.md) | Blame | Tognazzini and Coates (2014, rev. 2024). Blame. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. A survey organised by two questions: which reactions constitute blame, and when blaming is appropriate. Accounts of what blame is are sorted into cognitive (Smart, Watson's aretaic blame, Hieronymi), emotional (Strawson, Wallace), conative (Sher, and Scanlon's modification of a relationship impaired by the wrong) and functional (protest, communication). Each is reported with its main objections: Wallace's charge that Scanlon "leaves the blame out of blame", and the problem of blaming strangers. Appropriateness depends on facts about the person blamed (agency, freedom, including coercion and manipulation), about the blaming interaction (proportionality, evidence) and about the blamer (standing: hypocrisy, complicity, meddling, moral luck, and Carbonell's claimant injustice). Read as the stand-in for Scanlon's Moral Dimensions and beside [LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md) for Strawson. | Active — read 2026-11-16 ([NOTE-1998](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1998.md)) from the plato.stanford.edu HTML, substantive revision of 30 Aug 2024; filed and read as the stand-in for Scanlon, Moral Dimensions ([LIT-2694](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2694.md), Unavailable), and as a second neighbour, beside [LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md), for Strawson, "Freedom and Resentment" ([LIT-2679](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2679.md), Unfetched). It reports Scanlon's account of blame with page references (2008: 128–29) and its main criticisms, and Strawson's place as the source of emotional theories of blame. |
